rules.shared_requires: drug arm: at least 3 studies with a significantly raised ratio, and more raised than lowered; heat arm: at least 2 studies, at least one with explicitly high heat that does not point the protective way

tiers.direct: drug and heat studied together (curated, abstract-checked)
tiers.shared: drug linked to the effect and heat linked to the same effect, in different studies
tiers.direct_misuse: drug and heat studied together, but for drug use or overdose
tiers.weak: drug arm below threshold or no heat arm; not drawn by default
tiers.guidance_only: added in phase 2 from guidance documents

meta.outside_sources: guidance, effect_actions, specialties, scenarios and gaps come from outside the graph

effects.label: Ketoacidosis and high blood sugar crises

direct.finding: Admission for heat-related illness during the August 2003 heat wave in France was more likely in people taking anticholinergics (case-control study).
direct.note: Graph collapses three drug classes into one label; the abstract assigns 6.0 to anticholinergics (C10).

direct.finding: Admission for heat-related illness during the August 2003 heat wave in France was more likely in people taking antipsychotics (case-control study).
direct.note: Label corrected from the abstract (C10).

direct.finding: Admission for heat-related illness during the August 2003 heat wave in France was more likely in people taking anxiolytics (case-control study).
direct.note: The paper says anxiolytics; mapped to the opioids and sedatives class, which holds the benzodiazepines. Label corrected from the abstract (C10).

direct.finding: Among 83 heatstroke patients in Lyon in 2003, long-term antihypertensive use was associated with higher mortality.
direct.note: Antihypertensives studied as one group; no single class is named.

direct.finding: In about 2 million US insulin users aged 65 and over, serious hypoglycemia was more likely on days above the 99th percentile of heat index than on days at the 25th-74th percentile. The pattern was similar in Taiwan.
direct.graph_label: ambient heat (measured by heat index percentile)
direct.note: Found through the study population (route 3), not the variable names. Graph row holds the 95th-98th band, 1.14 (1.08-1.20). Heat bands from the abstract are in levels.

levels.measure: heat index percentile, compared with the 25th-74th percentile

direct.finding: Insulin disappeared from the injection site 50-60% faster at 35 °C than at 20 °C (6 patients).
direct.note: Extracted value (mean difference -10.0) does not match the abstract; quote the abstract (C11). Absorption mechanism for the dose-adjustment bucket.

direct.finding: A refrigerated insulin mixture gave an earlier and higher insulin peak than the same mixture stored unrefrigerated (7 patients with type 1 diabetes).
direct.note: Storage temperature changes how a mixed insulin acts. The only storage finding in the graph.

direct.finding: Among patients taking antihypertensives in the Arizona desert, 40.5% of syncope cases in summer were caused by dehydration, against 29% in winter (p = 0.04). The type of antihypertensive made no difference.
direct.graph_label: residence in a hot and dry climate (Sonoran desert) during summer months
direct.note: Found through the study population (route 3). Authors recommend judicious reduction of antihypertensives in hot, dry climates.

direct.finding: Irbesartan with hydrochlorothiazide lowered systolic blood pressure 3.9 mmHg less at 8 weeks when started in spring or summer than when started in autumn or winter (501 patients, China).
direct.note: Seasonal blood pressure response, not harm. Relevant to dose review in summer.

direct.finding: Monthly cases of thiazide-induced hyponatremia did not correlate with air temperature (r = -0.056, p = 0.65; 201 cases, Hong Kong).
direct.note: A null result. Show it.

direct.finding: Reports of drug-induced hyponatremia to Sweden's medicines agency rose with outdoor temperature: cumulative odds ratio 2.21 at a mean daily temperature of 20 °C, lag 1-3 days.
direct.note: Drugs not separated by class.

direct.finding: In lithium users, higher temperature on the day of testing trended toward a lower dose-to-level ratio (beta -0.17, p = 0.08). The authors judged it of little clinical importance in temperate climates and called for study above 40 °C.
direct.note: Near-null.

direct.finding: Emergency visits for opioid overdose in California rose as daily mean temperature went from the 50th to the 95th percentile (2005-2019).
direct.note: Drug use and overdose; not prescribed use.

direct.finding: Emergency visits for amphetamine overdose in California rose as daily mean temperature went from the 50th to the 95th percentile (2005-2019).
direct.note: Drug use and overdose; not prescribed use.

direct.finding: Emergency visits for cocaine overdose in California rose as daily mean temperature went from the 50th to the 95th percentile (2005-2019).
direct.note: Illicit use. Cocaine sits in the stimulants class.

direct.finding: A maximum weekly temperature of 30 °C, compared with 20 °C, was associated with death from cocaine overdose; not with other drug overdoses (OR 1.03).
direct.note: Illicit use.

direct.finding: In non-slum households in Odisha, India, people taking medication were more likely to have had heat illness.
direct.note: Medication not specified.

direct.finding: In long-distance cyclists, the number of current medications did not predict exertional heat illness.
direct.note: A null result.

direct.finding: Among people aged 70-100 in France, antipsychotic use was associated with death during the 2003 heat wave (population-based case-control).
direct.graph_label: therapeutic classes independently associated with death
direct.note: Found by the teammate's pipeline (heat in the study context, not the variables). Effect modified by temperature; dose-response with number of psychotropics (aOR 1.25 per drug).

direct.finding: Among people aged 70-100 in France, antidepressant use was associated with death during the 2003 heat wave (population-based case-control).
direct.graph_label: therapeutic classes independently associated with death
direct.note: Same study as d19. Anxiolytics/hypnotics were associated with lower odds (aOR 0.85).

actions.text: Consider adjusting medication dose or frequency in hot weather, individualised and drug-class dependent, weighing risks and benefits.
Consider adjusting fluid restrictions on hot days for patients on medicines that cause dehydration or affect electrolytes.
Remind patients not to stop medicines abruptly without a plan; document adjustments and when to resume the normal schedule.
Review regimens, especially multiple drugs that add to heat risk; discuss symptoms, emergencies and a point of contact for older patients and those with altered cognition.
Insulin can be degraded by heat and should be refrigerated; inhalers can burst and epinephrine auto-injectors may underdose in heat; do not leave medicines in a car; plan for power outages.
Consider adjusting medication dose or frequency during hot weather months; individualised and drug-class dependent.
Consider adjusting fluid restrictions on hot days for patients on medicines that cause dehydration or electrolyte changes.
Avoid stopping medicines abruptly without a plan; review the medication list with the patient; name a point of contact; plan for hot days and when to seek care.
Do not leave medicines in a car; insulin may lose effect in heat; inhalers and epinephrine auto-injectors can fail; power outage plan for refrigerated medicines.
For people on medicines that impair thermoregulation or cause dehydration, adjust regimens as needed on hot days.
Recommend self-monitoring of hydration.
People with diabetes should check their blood sugar more frequently in high temperatures.
actions.section: Some medical conditions increase heat vulnerability

actions.text: Review medicines that may affect thermoregulation; discuss symptoms of heat illness; advise more fluids when medically appropriate; air conditioning or a cool space.
actions.section: Some medical conditions increase heat vulnerability

actions.text: Use of antihypertensives during extreme heat events should be optimised as much as possible.
Monitor patient hydration (also named for cholinesterase inhibitors, antiarrhythmics, nitrates).
Topiramate: watch for hyperthermia and heat intolerance; oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine: precautions against hyponatremia, which needs close monitoring.
Lithium: hydrate with water rather than electrolyte solutions (risk of hypernatremia).
Drink water or electrolyte solutions through the day; protect from heat.
Minimising heat exposure is the best course; caution about the risks of changing treatment; consult the prescriber before summer begins.
Know proper insulin storage: vials at 32 °C can lose 14-18% potency over 28 days.
Identify patients and medications that raise heat risk; give heat-health information; discuss safe handling of heat-sensitive medicines.
The medicines list is a prompt to consider action and assess the risks and benefits of any changes.
actions.section: Medications with increased risk during hot weather

actions.text: Monitor fluid intake, for example by monitoring body weight.
Keep most medicines below 25 °C, out of direct sunlight; refrigerate only if specified.
Do not give aspirin or paracetamol to someone with heatstroke while waiting for an ambulance.
Not recommended in strong heat for fever or unusual pain: aspirin, paracetamol, NSAIDs (NSAID kidney toxicity rises with dehydration).
Reducing or stopping interacting medicines is not justified systematically; list each patient's medicines, identify those that impair heat adaptation and reassess the value of each.
Assess and check the patient's dehydration status.
Insulin: risk of hypoglycaemia from faster absorption in heat; transdermal patches may detach.
2-8 °C medicines stay refrigerated with temperature checks; below-25/30 °C medicines tolerate a few days' excursion; glucose meters and strips protected from heat.
Advise patients on any changes to medication dosage and fluid restrictions during extreme heat.
actions.section: Assess patients' risk from medications and medical conditions

guidance_sources.name: CDC: Heat and Medications, Guidance for Clinicians
guidance_sources.note: States that it reflects expert opinion and that its table is not comprehensive. Mechanisms for about 35 classes; class-specific actions only for sun-sensitising antimicrobials. General steps apply to every class.

guidance_sources.name: NYC Health: Heat and Medications (provider page)
guidance_sources.note: Medication table mirrors CDC almost word for word. Adds a non-drug checklist: AC access and cost, 78 °F setting, cooling centres (311), HEAP cooling assistance, a named check-in contact.

guidance_sources.name: Arizona (ADHS / SCORCH): Heat and Medications Information Sheet for Health Care Providers
guidance_sources.note: Consolidated drug-name list taken from CDC, plus insulin. No mechanisms per drug. General steps: fluid-intake advice, assess dose changes, buddy plan, cooling centres, utility assistance.

guidance_sources.name: UKHSA: Supporting vulnerable people before and during hot weather: healthcare professionals
guidance_sources.note: Mechanism list only; asks clinicians to assess risks and benefits of any change. Most medicines should be kept below 25 °C. Monitor fluid intake, for example by body weight. Also names colchicine, digoxin, immunosuppressants, chemotherapy, thyroxine.

guidance_sources.name: Health Canada: Extreme Heat Events Guidelines: Technical Guide for Health Care Workers
guidance_sources.note: The only source with class-specific monitoring actions (Table 4.2). Insulin vials at 32 °C lost 14–18% potency over 28 days. Chapters 3–4 read verbatim; later chapters not coded.

guidance_sources.name: ANSM (with CRPV Toulouse): Liste des médicaments pouvant diminuer l'adaptation de l'organisme aux vagues de chaleur
guidance_sources.note: Most complete list, organised by mechanism. The only source naming SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin/sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists and statins. Warns that patch delivery changes with heat and sweating. No class actions.

guidance_sources.name: ADAPT-HEAT study: CALOR list of heat-potentially inadequate medications (Germany)
guidance_sources.note: Only the study protocol is published (Bunz M et al., Methods Protoc 2026;9(3):78, PMID 42347031, CC BY). The Delphi consensus list has not been released; the study runs to December 2026. No drug-level recommendations exist yet.

guidance_sources.name: WHO Regional Office for Europe: Heat–health action plans: guidance, second edition
guidance_sources.note: Frames medicines as a health-system task: pre-season medication reviews for patients on diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, antidepressants and lithium (p. 214); at-risk registers that include medication use (pp. 90, 209); storage and supply checks for temperature-sensitive medicines (pp. 134, 212).
